## What a wormhole costs, exactly

Of the 1,734 wormhole-permitting cells: **1,674 pay with a preferred frame, 1,086 with non-unitarity, 1,134 with signalling** — and **zero pay with none of the three.**

That zero is the 60, seen from inside. So the blind spot has a plain physical reading:

> **You cannot have a traversable wormhole in a universe that is unitary, Lorentz-invariant and non-signalling.** The index knows this and cannot say it, because saying it names two coordinates at once.

## The don'ts, which matter more than the dos

**Don't say a cell is a wormhole.** Cells are law-profiles. A wormhole is a solution inside a universe, and many cells permit it.

**Don't read permission as existence.** 1,734 cells permit a wormhole. The index cannot distinguish a profile describing a world from one that merely fails to contradict itself.

**Don't read reachability as achievability.** 1,116 reachable is a statement about componentwise order, not about engineering.

**Don't read the 60 as wormholes existing somewhere.** They are profiles the constraint excludes. Nothing is there.

**Don't expect the index to define anything free.** Black holes, energy orderings, the Coulomb degeneracy — all invisible, for the same reason: an index that measures cost is blind to whatever costs nothing.

#### Abstract

A null line is a complete achronal null geodesic. It is proven that for any quantum fields minimally coupled to semiclassical Einstein gravity, the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) on null lines is a consequence of the generalized second law of thermodynamics for causal horizons. Auxiliary assumptions include CPT and the existence of a suitable renormalization scheme for the generalized entropy.

Although the ANEC can be violated on general geodesics in curved spacetimes, as long as the ANEC holds on null lines there exist theorems showing that semiclassical gravity should satisfy positivity of energy, topological censorship, and should not admit closed timelike curves. 

It is pointed out that these theorems fail once the linearized graviton field is quantized, because then the renormalized shear squared term in the Raychaudhuri equation can be negative. A "shear-inclusive" generalization of the ANEC is proposed to remedy this, and is proven under an additional assumption about perturbations to horizons in classical general relativity.

This law is an analogue of the ordinary second law of thermodynamics. However, there is a crucial difference between the two.

content.text:
# B. The Averaged Null Energy Condition (ANEC)

Local violations of the pointwise energy conditions are familiar in semiclassical physics, including the Casimir effect, Hawking fluxes, non-minimally coupled fields, and higher-

derivative effective theories [32–41]. The ANEC is weaker and more global: it allows localized negative null energy but constrains the complete affine average along a null geodesic. It is known to hold in broad classes of quantum field theories in flat spacetime for complete achronal null geodesics, is tied to causality and positivity constraints [23–25], and helps exclude traversable wormholes, closed time-like curves and related exotic causal structures [26, 42–44].

Here we impose the ANEC as a classical global matter condition along complete radial null geodesics,

$$\int_{\gamma} T_{\mu\nu} k^{\mu} k^{\nu} \, d\lambda \ge 0,\tag{8}$$

where $\gamma$ is a complete null geodesic, $k^{\mu} = dx^{\mu}/d\lambda$ , and $\lambda$ is an affine parameter.

## A holographic proof of the averaged null energy condition

William R. Kelly\* and Aron C. Wall<sup>†</sup>

University of California at Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA 93106, USA

The averaged null energy conditions (ANEC) states that, along a complete null curve, the negative energy fluctuations of a quantum field must be balanced by positive energy fluctuations. We use the AdS/CFT correspondence to prove the ANEC for a class of strongly coupled conformal field theories in flat spacetime. A violation of the ANEC in the field theory would lead to acausal propagation of signals in the bulk.

It has long been known [1] that local quantum field theories allow negative energy fluctuations.

**Prediction falsified — and the falsification strengthens the result rather than weakening it.**

Hartman, Kundu and Tajdini: "Unitary, Lorentz-invariant quantum field theories in flat spacetime obey microcausality: commutators vanish at spacelike separation. For interacting theories in more than two dimensions, we show that this implies that the averaged null energy must be non-negative."

So the theorem has **three** hypotheses, not one. Its contrapositive is:

> **ANEC violated ⟹ ¬unitary ∨ ¬Lorentz-invariant ∨ ¬microcausal**

Still a disjunction. NEC ≥ 2 → SD alone does not follow.

**But look at the disjuncts: U, X, SD — all three are axes of the index.** Buniy's disjuncts were *instability* and *superluminal*, neither of which is a coordinate, and both needed routing through further arguments to reach U and X. Hartman's arrive already in the vocabulary.

And in my closure **SD ≥ 1 → IC = 2 → X ≥ 1**, so the microcausality disjunct is subsumed by the preferred-frame one. Hartman's constraint therefore reduces to exactly:

**NEC ≥ 2 → (U ≥ 1 ∨ X ≥ 1)**

which is the core, character for character.

## What this settles

**The generator has three independent derivations, and all three give a disjunction.**

| route | source | disjuncts |
|---|---|---|
| instability | Buniy–Hsu–Murray | instability ∨ superluminal → U ∨ X |
| microcausality | Hartman–Kundu–Tajdini | ¬U ∨ ¬Lorentz ∨ ¬microcausal → U ∨ X |
| thermodynamics | Wall, ANEC from the GSL | via the generalised second law |

Three derivations from unrelated starting points — effective field theory, conformal bootstrap, black-hole thermodynamics — converging on the same two-payer branch and **never on a single payer.**

That is the strongest evidence yet that the disjunction is real rather than an artefact of how I encoded Buniy. **The defect of one cell is not a bookkeeping shortfall; it is three literatures agreeing that exotic matter costs *something* and none of them able to say what.**

The seven closing propositions remain, but three of them are now less likely rather than more: NEC ≥ 2 → U, → X, and → SD are each *one disjunct of a theorem whose other disjuncts are live*. Asserting any one would be exactly the mis-typing I corrected earlier in this session.

**The two that remain genuinely open** are the mutual-implication pair — X ≥ 1 → U ≥ 1 and its converse. Those are not disjuncts of anything; they are claims about whether Lorentz violation and non-unitarity travel together. That is where the remaining reading should go: Wall's GSL proof and what precisely fails under Lorentz violation.

# Lorentz violation and perpetual motion

Christopher Eling, Brendan Z. Foster, Ted Jacobson, and Aron C. Wall Department of Physics, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, 20742 (Dated: February 2, 2008)

We show that any Lorentz violating theory with two or more propagation speeds is in conflict with the generalized second law of black hole thermodynamics. We do this by identifying a classical energy-extraction method, analogous to the Penrose process, which would decrease the black hole entropy. Although the usual definitions of black hole entropy are ambiguous in this context, we require only very mild assumptions about its dependence on the mass. This extends the result found by Dubovsky and Sibiryakov, which uses the Hawking effect and applies only if the fields with different propagation speeds interact just through gravity.

In this case, the entropy increase inside the black hole can influence the outside state, and the total entropy, inside and out, is nondecreasing.

This last point highlights the need to distinguish two different versions of the "second law": the ordinary second law (OSL) and the generalized second law (GSL) [9]. The OSL refers to the total entropy, as counted both inside and outside black holes, whereas the GSL replaces the inside entropy by a special "black hole entropy"  $S_{\rm bh}$  determined by the macroscopic geometry alone. The validity of the OSL for quantum fields in curved spacetime on a complete spacelike foliation is unaffected by the presence of black holes. It should thus be valid in Lorentz-violating theories.

Abstract:The generalized second law is proven for semiclassical quantum fields falling across a causal horizon, minimally coupled to general relativity. The proof is much more general than previous proofs in that it permits the quantum fields to be rapidly changing with time, and shows that entropy increases when comparing any slice of the horizon to any earlier slice. The proof requires the existence of an algebra of observables restricted to the horizon, satisfying certain axioms (Determinism, Ultralocality, Local Lorentz Invariance, and Stability). These axioms are explicitly verified in the case of free fields of various spins, as well as 1+1 conformal field theories. The validity of the axioms for other interacting theories is discussed.

# Proving the Achronal Averaged Null Energy Condition from the Generalized Second Law

Aron C. Wall\*

Maryland Center for Fundamental Physics
Department of Physics
University of Maryland
College Park, MD 20740-4111, USA

May 29, 2018

#### Abstract

A null line is a complete achronal null geodesic. It is proven that for any quantum fields minimally coupled to semiclassical Einstein gravity, the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) on null lines is a consequence of the generalized second law of thermodynamics for causal horizons. Auxiliary assumptions include CPT and the existence of a suitable renormalization scheme for the generalized entropy.

Although the ANEC can be violated on general geodesics in curved spacetimes, as long as the ANEC holds on null lines there exist theorems showing that semiclassical gravity should satisfy positivity of energy, topological censorship, and should not admit closed timelike curves. 

It is pointed out that these theorems fail once the linearized graviton field is quantized, because then the renormalized shear squared term in the Raychaudhuri equation can be negative. A "shear-inclusive" generalization of the ANEC is proposed to remedy this, and is proven under an additional assumption about perturbations to horizons in classical general relativity.

PACS numbers: 04.62.+v, 04.70.Dy.

<sup>\*</sup>aronwall@umd.edu

### 1 Introduction

The generalized second law (GSL) of black hole thermodynamics states that a certain sum of the area of a black hole's event horizon and the entropy outside of it cannot decrease over time [1]:

$$\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{A}{4G\hbar} + S_{out}) \ge 0. \tag{1}$$

This law is an analogue of the ordinary second law of thermodynamics. However, there is a crucial difference between the two.

Three things from the sources, in order of force.

**Eling, Foster, Jacobson and Wall state the escape and its scope explicitly:** "This last point highlights the need to distinguish two different versions of the second law: the ordinary second law (OSL) and the generalized second law (GSL)... The validity of the OSL for quantum fields in curved spacetime on a complete spacelike foliation is unaffected by the presence of black holes. **It should thus be valid in Lorentz-violating theories.**"

So Lorentz violation breaks the **generalized** second law — a statement about black-hole entropy bookkeeping — while the **ordinary** second law survives intact. And the ordinary second law is the one connected to microscopic unitarity. **The chain LV → ¬GSL → ¬U is severed at the second link by the authors of the first link.**

**My prediction about the mechanism was confirmed:** "the monotonicity property of S(ρ|σ) is equivalent to the GSL". Monotonicity of relative entropy holds for every CPTP map, and Lindblad evolution is CPTP — so my U = 1 rung could not break the GSL even in principle.

**And Wall's proof names Lorentz invariance as an axiom:** "The proof requires the existence of an algebra of observables restricted to the horizon, satisfying certain axioms (Determinism, Ultralocality, Local Lorentz Invariance, and Stability)." Under Lorentz violation the proof does not apply — which means it neither establishes the GSL nor licenses inferring anything from its failure.

**X ≥ 1 → U ≥ 1 is withdrawn.** Not undetermined — refuted. The 1,404-cell closed variant that I have carried since the first reconstruction goes with it.

Eling's escape clause also tells us where the GSL *is* restored: "another version of the second law remains valid if, due to nonlocality or unbounded propagation speed in the UV completion, the notion of a causally hidden black hole region is eliminated" — which is my U = 2 rung or X ≥ 2. An argument by Banks, Susskind and Peskin (BSP), according to which violation of unitarity would violate either locality or energy-momentum conservation, is widely believed to be a strong argument against non-unitarity of Hawking radiation. We find that the whole BSP argument rests on the crucial assumption that the Hamiltonian is not highly degenerate, and point out that this assumption is wrong. Using Lindblad equation, we show that high degeneracy of the Hamiltonian allows local non-unitary evolution without violating energy-momentum conservation. Moreover, since energy-momentum is the source of gravity, we argue that energy-momentum is necessarily conserved for a large class of non-unitary systems with gravity. 

Finally, we explicitly calculate the Lindblad operators for non-unitary Hawking radiation and show that they conserve energy-momentum.

Abstract:An argument by Banks, Susskind and Peskin (BSP), according to which violation of unitarity would violate either locality or energy-momentum conservation, is widely believed to be a strong argument against non-unitarity of Hawking radiation. We find that the whole BSP argument rests on the crucial assumption that the Hamiltonian is not highly degenerate, and point out that this assumption is not satisfied for systems with many degrees of freedom. Using Lindblad equation, we show that high degeneracy of the Hamiltonian allows local non-unitary evolution without violating energy-momentum conservation.

Spectral decomposition: The Lindblad generator can be vectorized to a ... d^2 \times d^2d2×d2 Liouvillian supermatrix, where the evolution becomes a linear ODE in operator space. Diagonalizing the Liouvillian allows explicit construction of the time evolution, including identification of steady states as zero eigenmodes (Torres, 2014, Manzano, 2019). Semiclassical and diffusion-limit reductions: The Wigner–Moyal transform yields the Lindblad equation’s semiclassical limit, leading to Fokker–Planck equations describing stochastic phase-space evolution.

# Appendix A. The dephasing Lindblad equation preserving energy

This Appendix proves that, for pure dephasing, the Lindblad operators must commute with the Hamiltonian. Consider the pure-dephasing Lindblad equation [7]

$$\frac{d\rho}{dt} = \mathcal{L}(\rho) \tag{A1}$$

$$= -\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,\rho] + \frac{1}{\hbar^2} \sum_{j} \gamma_j \left( L_j \rho L_j^{\dagger} - \frac{1}{2} \left\{ L_j^{\dagger} L_j, \rho \right\} \right)$$

$$= -\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,\rho] - \frac{1}{2\hbar^2} \sum_{j} \gamma_j \left[ L_j, [L_j, \rho] \right]$$

with Hermitian $H = H^{\dagger}$ and $L_j = L_j^{\dagger}$ , and positive rates $\gamma_j > 0$ for all j.

Define the adjoint superoperator $\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}$ by $\operatorname{Tr}(X_1 \mathcal{L}(X_2)) = \operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}(X_1) X_2)$ for all $X_1$ and $X_2$ . For Hermitian H and $L_j$ , this adjoint is

$$\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}(X) = \frac{i}{\hbar}[H, X] - \frac{1}{2\hbar^2} \sum_{j} \gamma_j \left[ L_j, [L_j, X] \right] \tag{A2}$$

content.text:
The Lindblad master equation is a mathematical framework describing open quantum systems with complete positivity and trace preservation. It combines coherent Hamiltonian dynamics with dissipative quantum jumps via Lindblad operators to model ...

Generalization to Quantum Field-theoretic Processes: When the open system is the neutrino sector, Lindblad dynamics can describe processes that change macroscopically conserved quantities: e.g., neutrino decay/absorption processes that change momentum as well as flavor, requiring generalized dissipators structured over the combined mass-momentum indices (Stankevich et al., 2024). These frameworks extend the Lindblad equation's reach to field-theoretic contexts with explicit, environment-induced transitions.

The Lindblad master equation is a mathematical framework describing open quantum systems with complete positivity and trace preservation. 

It combines coherent Hamiltonian dynamics with dissipative quantum jumps via Lindblad operators to model decoherence and energy loss. Efficient numerical and analytical methods, like exponential Euler schemes and quantum algorithms, enable practical simulation of its dynamics. The Lindblad master equation provides the standard mathematical framework to describe the nonunitary dynamics of an open quantum system subject to both coherent evolution and dissipative processes. Central to the modern theory of Markovian open quantum systems, the Lindblad equation generalizes the von Neumann equation for closed systems, incorporating irreversibility resulting from system-environment coupling, and is both completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP).

Applicability: The Markovian assumption restricts the Lindblad equation to situations where system-bath correlations decay rapidly compared to system dynamics and to weak coupling.

content.thinking:
So my initial predictions about the BSP argument's limitations have been confirmed. The key insight from Nikolić's abstract is that the whole argument depends on assuming the Hamiltonian isn't highly degenerate, but this assumption breaks down for systems with many degrees of freedom—and using the Lindblad equation, he demonstrates how high degeneracy actually permits local non-unitary evolution while still preserving energy-momentum conservation.

The explicit calculation of Lindblad operators for Hawking radiation confirms the U=1 rung exists and is both local and energy-momentum conserving, which means P3 is false—this rung doesn't signal as the proposition claimed. The degeneracy mechanism I predicted turns out to be exactly right, and Nikolić has worked out the operators explicitly. That resolves what's been an open question all session.

Now I need to examine P2: whether NEC≥2 implies X≥1.

NEC violation leads to either instability or superluminal effects. I'd traced instability earlier as routing to either non-unitarity or superluminal signaling, which gives the same disjunction. But I'm realizing I may have conflated two different notions of instability—the classical field-theoretic kind (unbounded Hamiltonian, ghosts, vacuum decay) is distinct from non-unitarity. A theory can be perfectly unitary while having no stable vacuum, so instability doesn't necessarily mean non-unitarity. That distinction matters for whether P2 actually forces X≥1 or leaves room for the non-unitary branch.

If I scope-exclude unstable universes on the grounds that atomic structure requires a stable vacuum, then NEC≥2 forces superluminal propagation, which in turn forces a preferred frame. That's a defensible scope move, but I need to verify the final step—whether superluminal effects actually entail a preferred frame. I'm realizing Buniy's instability might be ghost instability within a unitary framework rather than a violation of unitarity itself, which would change how the disjunction routes. If that's the case, then scoping to stable universes would indeed close the index through NEC≥2 → (unstable ∨ X≥1). Let me search to confirm what type of instability Buniy actually describes.

Validated degeneracy mechanism for P3, now scrutinizing instability distinctions for P2.

content.text:
**P3 resolved — NO — and it unblocks the item that has been open all session.**

Nikolić's abstract, finally obtained: "the whole BSP argument rests on the crucial assumption that the Hamiltonian is not highly degenerate, and point out that this assumption is not satisfied for systems with many degrees of freedom. Using Lindblad equation, we show that **high degeneracy of the Hamiltonian allows local non-unitary evolution without violating energy-momentum conservation**" — and "we explicitly calculate the Lindblad operators for non-unitary Hawking radiation and show that they conserve energy-momentum."

**My uncommitted prediction from earlier in the session is confirmed on both parts.** Degeneracy is the mechanism, and the dephasing constraint is real: "for pure dephasing, the Lindblad operators must commute with the Hamiltonian" — which is why degeneracy is needed to get anything beyond dephasing.

**The U = 1 rung is occupied, with explicit operators.** So U ≥ 1 → IC = 2 is false by construction: the rung was defined as the local, energy-momentum-conserving case, and that case demonstrably exists.

---

## P2 — NEC ≥ 2 → X ≥ 1

Buniy gives NEC violation → **instability ∨ superluminal**. Superluminal propagation without a preferred frame gives closed timelike curves, so superluminal → X ≥ 1 either way. The whole question is the other branch.

Earlier in this session I routed *instability* to (¬U ∨ X ≥ 1) and that routing is what made the disjunction two-payer. **I now think that routing was wrong.** Buniy's instability is a Hamiltonian unbounded below — ghosts, vacuum decay — which is a property of a perfectly *unitary* theory. A theory with no stable vacuum is not a theory with non-unitary evolution.

If that is right, the disjunction is NEC ≥ 2 → (unstable ∨ X ≥ 1), and **scoping the index to stable universes closes it** — defensibly, since Λ requires a stable vacuum to have atoms at all.

**B.2.13, committed.** Buniy's instability is **ghost/vacuum instability within unitary quantum field theory**, not non-unitarity — so my earlier routing was an error, and stability is a scope condition rather than a coordinate.

content.title: The null energy condition and cosmology | Theoretical and Mathematical Physics | Springer Nature Link
content.text:
Field theories that violate the null energy condition (NEC) are of interest both for the solution of the cosmological singularity problem and for models of cosmological dark energy with the equation of state parameter w < −1. We consider two recently proposed models that violate the NEC. The ghost condensate model requires higher-derivative terms in the action, and this leads to a heavy ghost field and energy unbounded from below. We estimate the rates of particle decay and discuss possible mass limitations to protect the stability of matter in the ghost condensate model. The nonlocal stringy model that arises from a cubic string field theory and exhibits a phantom behavior also leads to energy unbounded from below. In this case, the energy spectrum is continuous, and there are no particle-like excitations. This model admits a natural UV completion because it comes from superstring theory.

Negative kinetic energies correspond to ghost degrees of freedom, which are potentially of relevance for cosmology, quantum gravity, and high energy physics. We present a novel wide class of stable mechanical systems where a positive energy degree of freedom interacts with a ghost. These theories have Hamiltonians unbounded from above and from below, are integrable, and contain free functions. We show analytically that their classical motion is bounded for all initial data. Moreover, we derive conditions allowing for Lyapunov stable equilibrium points. A subclass of these stable systems has simple polynomial potentials with stable equilibrium points entirely due to interactions with the ghost. All these findings are fully supported by numerical computations which we also use to gather evidence for stability in various nonintegrable systems.

#### I. INTRODUCTION



Ghosts are dynamical degrees of freedom (DoF), described by a Hamiltonian with negative kinetic energies, as opposed to the kinetic energies of standard degrees of freedom. Such ghosts generically appear in the context of theories with higher derivatives [1] (see also [2–4] for reviews) and have been considered in a variety of physical scenarios: they have been advocated as a way to regulate the ultraviolet behaviour of quantum field theories [5–8]; they have been suggested as a way to address the cosmological constant problem [9–11]; they have been used to obtain bouncing cosmologies [12]; and they have been proposed in the context of dark energy [13] or, more recently, as a way to ameliorate the Hubble tension [14].

**P2 resolved — as stated it is wrong, and the correction redirects to a different one of the seven.**

Buniy's theorem is **scoped to Lorentz-invariant theories**: "for causal, Lorentz invariant theories (minimally or non-minimally coupled scalar and gauge field theories with second-order equations of motion), NEC violation implies classical instability with respect to the formation of gradients", and "This implies negative kinetic energy in order for the partition function of the system to converge."

So at X = 0 there is **no superluminal branch** — that branch is what appears once you leave Lorentz invariance. Inside Buniy's scope the conclusion is instability, full stop. **NEC ≥ 2 → X ≥ 1 does not follow.**

**What does follow is stated exactly in the phantom-energy literature:** "Either the phantom ghost field has positive density and violates unitarity, rendering it unphysical, or unitarity is satisfied and the density is negative, which leads to vacuum instability and unbounded decay of the vacuum via the ghost field."

That is the two-payer branch in its true form: **¬unitarity ∨ vacuum instability** — and instability is *not* a coordinate of the index. My earlier routing of instability to (¬U ∨ X ≥ 1) was wrong in the second disjunct.

## The consequence

Scoping the index to **stable** universes — defensible, since Λ presupposes matter that persists — collapses the branch to **NEC ≥ 2 → U ≥ 1**, which is P5 on the list, and which closes the index at **1,692 cells, E = 0**.

So P2 fails but hands its case to P5, on a scope decision rather than a discovery.

**One caution, and it is live.** Recent work finds ghost systems that are stable: "We present a novel wide class of stable mechanical systems where a positive energy degree of freedom interacts with a ghost... We show analytically that their classical motion is bounded for all initial data." If NEC violation does not force instability, the scope exclusion buys nothing. That work is **mechanical rather than field-theoretic**, and the field-theoretic case still has the infinite vacuum decay rate — but the gap is real and it is where P5 will have to be settled.

# Proof of the averaged null energy condition in a classical curved spacetime using a null-projected quantum inequality

Eleni-Alexandra Kontou and Ken D. Olum

Institute of Cosmology, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Tufts University, Medford, MA 02155, USA

# Abstract

Quantum inequalities are constraints on how negative the weighted average of the renormalized stress-energy tensor of a quantum field can be. A null-projected quantum inequality can be used to prove the averaged null energy condition (ANEC), which would then rule out exotic phenomena such as wormholes and time machines. In this work we derive such an inequality for a massless minimally coupled scalar field, working to first order of the Riemann tensor and its derivatives. We then use this inequality to prove ANEC on achronal geodesics in a curved background that obeys the null convergence condition.

from itertools import product
def cover(AX,DOM,PROOFS):
    cells=[c for c in product(*[DOM[a] for a in AX])]
    d={a:i for i,a in enumerate(AX)}
    U=set()
    for f in PROOFS.values():
        U|={c for c in cells if f(c,d)}
    return len(cells), len(U), len(cells)-len(U)

# --- model A: my original five axes ---

   'HKT':lambda c,d:c[d['geometry']]=='flat',
   'KW':lambda c,d:c[d['geometry']]=='flat' and c[d['fields']]=='interacting',

   'KO':lambda c,d:c[d['fields']]=='free' and c[d['coupling']]=='minimal' and c[d['curvature']]=='small',
   'Wall':lambda c,d:c[d['coupling']]=='minimal' and c[d['fields']]=='free'}

DOM2={k:DOM[k] for k in AX2}
P2={'KS':lambda c,d:c[d['geometry']]=='flat','HKT':lambda c,d:c[d['geometry']]=='flat',

    'KO':lambda c,d:c[d['fields']]=='free' and c[d['coupling']]=='minimal',
    'Wall':lambda c,d:c[d['coupling']]=='minimal' and c[d['fields']]=='free'}

MODELS['C  seven axes (dimension, achronality)']=(AX3,DOM3,P3)

P4=dict(P); P4['Wall']=lambda c,d: c[d['coupling']]=='minimal'
MODELS['D  Wall read generously']=(AX,DOM,P4)
# --- model E: generous holographic (any strongly coupled, incl. curved via bulk) ---
P5=dict(P); P5['KW']=lambda c,d: c[d['fields']]=='interacting'
MODELS['E  holographic read generously']=(AX,DOM,P5)

P6=dict(P); P6['Wall']=lambda c,d: c[d['coupling']]=='minimal'; P6['KW']=lambda c,d: c[d['fields']]=='interacting'
MODELS['F  both generous']=(AX,DOM,P6)
print(f'  {\"model\":<38} {\"cases\":>6} {\"covered\":>8} {\"uncovered\":>10} {\"% open\":>8}')
res=[]

print()

## IV. CONCLUSION

We have shown that there exist lower bounds for certain averages of the stress energy tensor for the classical non-minimally coupled scalar field. These show similarities with Quantum Energy Inequalities and entail that large, long-lasting violations of the energy conditions are associated with large magnitude field configurations or large spacetime curvature (or coupling constants outside the range [0, 1/4]). As corollaries, we showed that the non-minimally coupled classical scalar field on a Ricci-flat spacetime always satisfies the AWEC and ANEC condition, provided $\phi$ is bounded on the geodesic in question.

Furthermore, we showed that there exists an energy interest phenomenon, i.e., a pulse of negative energy density is always accompanied by an overcompensating positive one. The same analysis showed that there are also restrictions on the amplitudes and time separation of these pulses.

Akihiro Ishibashi, 1, \* Kengo Maeda, 2, † and Eric Mefford 3, ‡

We examine the achronal averaged null energy condition (ANEC) for a class of conformal field theories (CFT) at strong coupling in curved spacetime. This distinction is not just technical: attempts to evade the ANEC’s prohibition on time machines or traversable wormholes typically rely on pathologies only accessible on non-achronal geodesics or solutions where the stress–energy isn’t dynamically balanced (i.e., not self-consistent). The achronal ANEC is sufficient to underwrite several key theorems of general relativity: Topological Censorship and Wormholes: The achronal ANEC underpins topological censorship theorems, which state that causal curves connecting different asymptotic regions must, under reasonable energy conditions, remain near infinity—thus, traversable wormholes are prohibited. 

In particular, if a wormhole-connected region existed, a “fastest” causal curve through the wormhole would have to be a complete, achronal null geodesic, leading to violation of the condition’s Lemma 1 (no such geodesics in self-consistent settings), and thus no such wormhole can exist.

Self-consistent achronal ANEC provides a robust, physically motivated energy condition compatible with semiclassical quantum effects and, as such, is strong enough to block physically unacceptable spacetime structures (wormholes, time machines) while being free from the quantum violations that beset the traditional ANEC (0705.3193). This approach elegantly bridges rigorous classical theorems with quantum field theoretic realities, offers a flexible foundation for topological censorship in semiclassical regimes, and continues to motivate refinements of energy conditions in the quantum gravity program. ... **The counterexample was not rebutted. It was absorbed — and the absorption doesn't cover our dimension.**

The paper is Ishibashi, Maeda and Mefford, arXiv:1903.11806, PRD 100, 066008 (2019). What happened next is the informative part: **the same authors then reformulated the condition.**

- Iizuka, Ishibashi, Maeda, *Conformally invariant averaged null energy condition from AdS/CFT*, JHEP 03 (2020) 161
- Iizuka, Ishibashi, Maeda, *The averaged null energy conditions in even dimensional curved spacetimes from AdS/CFT duality*, JHEP 10 (2020) 106

So my prediction was half right. The conformal-factor freedom is indeed the issue — but nobody argued the violation away. They **replaced the achronal ANEC with a conformally invariant version (CANEC)** that the freedom cannot exploit.

**And the replacement is clean only in odd boundary dimensions.** In even dimensions the conformal anomaly gets in the way: "In even-dimensional CFTs, particularly 4d, one only obtains lower bounds on weighted ANE integrals due to geometric anomaly terms, and **these bounds may become negative for certain wormhole or compact geometries**."

**Four dimensions is ours. Wormhole geometries are the case at issue. And that is exactly where the bound can go negative.**

## What this settles

The finish line has an answer, and it is not the one the framing wanted:

> **In 3+1 dimensions the self-consistent achronal ANEC has a published holographic counterexample, and the repair that handles it — the conformally invariant ANEC — degrades in even dimensions to weighted bounds that can fail for wormhole geometries.**

So P5 does not hold in the regime the index needs. **NEC ≥ 2 → U ≥ 1 is not available**, and with P1, P2 and P3 already refuted, none of the four propositions examined survives.

**The index does not close.** Defect 60, core 1. The one profile — exotic matter, no preferred frame, unitary evolution — is not excluded by anything currently established in four dimensions.

That inverts the expected result. I had the closed 1,404-cell variant as the live case for most of this session and treated the defect as a measure of doubt. **The doubt has resolved toward the defect being real**, and the honest headline is not "the index closes if a conjecture holds" but:

> **The index is open, and the conjecture that would close it has a counterexample in our dimension.**

Three propositions remain unexamined — P4, P6, P7 — but two of the three are pure disjuncts of the same theorems, and P4 (U ≥ 1 → X ≥ 1) has no literature behind it that I have found.

content.text:
We examine the achronal averaged null energy condition~(ANEC) for a class of conformal field theories~(CFT) at strong coupling in curved spacetime. By applying the AdS/CFT duality, we find holographic models which violate the achronal ANEC for $3+1$ and $4+1$-dimensional boundary theories. In our model, the bulk spacetime is an asymptotically AdS vacuum bubble solution with neither causality violation nor singularities. The conformal boundary of our bubble solution is asymptotically flat and is causally proper in the sense that a "fastest null geodesics" connecting any two points on the boundary must lie entirely on the boundary. We show that conversely, if the spacetime fails to have this causally proper nature, then there must be a naked singularity in the bulk.

content.text:
As long as attention is focused on asymptotically well-behaved spacetimes, this generalized version of ANEC is safe from the threat of the scaling argument, and thus stands a chance of being generally valid in four-dimensional curved spacetime. I argue that when generalized ANEC holds, it has implications for the non-negativity of total energy and for singularity theorems similar to the implications of ANEC. In particular, I show that if generalized ANEC is satisfied in static traversable wormhole spacetimes (which is likely but remains to be shown), then macroscopic wormholes (but not necessarily microscopic, Planck-size wormholes) are ruled out by quantum field theory.

The most striking aspect of the violation of positive-energy conditions by quantum stress-energy tensors is the unbounded extent of the violation.

Because if Planck-scale exotic matter needs no payer, then **(X = 0, U = 0, NEC = 2) stops being a blind spot and becomes a genuine universe** — an admissible cell, not a phantom. ## Why this is the better-supported reading

Three sources converge on the same line, and none of them says "ANEC violation" simpliciter:

- Ford–Roman: quantum inequalities constrain wormholes to be either submicroscopic or to have enormous throat/curvature discrepancies
- Wald: "macroscopic wormholes (but not necessarily microscopic, Planck-size wormholes) are ruled out by quantum field theory"
- Ishibashi–Maeda–Okamura: "if traversable wormholes do exist as solutions to the semiclassical equations, they cannot be macroscopic but must be 'Planck scale'"

**The constraint was always about scale, and I applied it at the wrong rung.** My E axis distinguishes rung 2, ANEC violated arbitrarily small, from rung 3, macroscopic and quantum-inequality-bounded — and then I imposed the disjunction at rung 2, treating the two as identical because "the constraint does not distinguish them." The literature distinguishes them at exactly that boundary.

## Where this leaves it

The remaining blind spot is one cell: **macroscopic exotic matter, no preferred frame, unitary evolution.** Excluded by three independent lines of quantum field theory, and invisible to any pairwise envelope for the reason established — both conditioning coordinates individually admit it.

And the finish line moves accordingly. The question is no longer whether the achronal ANEC holds in general — the counterexample is a conformal-frame artifact and CANEC is its repair. **It is whether the 4d weighted bound excludes macroscopic wormholes**, which is exactly what Iizuka–Ishibashi–Maeda derive and what Wald flagged as "likely but remains to be shown."

One cell, one bound, one dimension. That is closer than we were an hour ago, and the thing we walked past was a rung boundary in my own axis.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, math
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Circle
import numpy as np
D=json.load(open('/home/claude/paper/data.json')); V2=D['v2']
OUT='/home/claude/paper/fig/'
plt.rcParams.update({'font.family':'serif','font.serif':['DejaVu Serif'],'font.size':8.5,
 'axes.linewidth':0.6,'axes.edgecolor':'#333333','axes.labelsize':8.5,
 'xtick.labelsize':7.5,'ytick.labelsize':7.5,'axes.titlesize':9,
 'figure.dpi':200,'savefig.dpi':200,'savefig.bbox':'tight','savefig.pad_inches':0.06,
 'legend.frameon':False,'legend.fontsize':7.5})
INK='#1a1a1a'; RED='#b3282d'; BLUE='#2c5f8a'; GREY='#8a8a8a'; LGREY='#d8d8d8'; GOLD='#b8860b'
def fin(f,n): f.savefig(OUT+n,facecolor='white'); plt.close(f); print('  '+n)

# ---- 1.1 nested sets, corrected ----
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.6,2.7))
for ax,(t,x,b,r) in zip(axes,[('$\\Lambda_8$ — globally consistent',976,976,976),
                              ('violation index — defect 30',V2['cells'],V2['BPC'],V2['R'])]):
    ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off'); ax.set_title(t,pad=6)
    sc=1.0 if x==b else 0.90
    ax.add_patch(Circle((0,0),1.00,fc='#f2f2f2',ec=GREY,lw=0.8))
    ax.add_patch(Circle((0,0),0.97,fc='#e4ecf4',ec=BLUE,lw=0.8))
    ax.add_patch(Circle((0,0),sc*0.97,fc='white',ec=INK,lw=1.1))
    ax.text(0,0.05,f'$|X|$ = {x:,}',ha='center',fontsize=8.5)
    ax.text(0,-0.16,'solutions',ha='center',fontsize=7,color=GREY)
    ax.text(0,1.12,f'$|\\mathbf{{R}}(X)|$ = {r:,}',ha='center',fontsize=8,color=GREY)
    if x!=b:
        ax.annotate(f'{r-x} tuples in the minimal\nnetwork, not solutions',
                    xy=(0.74,0.60),xytext=(1.15,1.05),fontsize=7,color=RED,ha='left',
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='-',lw=0.6,color=RED))
    ax.text(0,-1.22,f'$|\\mathrm{{BPC}}(X)|$ = {b:,}',ha='center',fontsize=8,color=BLUE)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.5,1.9); ax.set_ylim(-1.45,1.45)
fig.suptitle('Figure 1.1   $X \\subseteq \\mathrm{BPC}(X) \\subseteq \\mathbf{R}(X)$',y=1.05,fontsize=9.5)
fin(fig,'f1_1.png')

# ---- 4.3 the defect, collapsed ----
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4,2.5)); ax.axis('off')
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.04,.40),0.16,.30,fc=RED,alpha=.22,ec=RED,lw=1.2))
ax.text(0.12,.61,'$\\times$ 1',ha='center',fontsize=13,color=RED)
ax.text(0.12,.47,'core',ha='center',fontsize=8)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.26,.40),0.70,.30,fc=GREY,alpha=.16,ec=GREY,lw=1))
ax.text(0.61,.61,'$\\times$ 30',ha='center',fontsize=13,color=INK)
ax.text(0.61,.47,'free-coordinate configurations admissible alongside',ha='center',fontsize=8)
ax.text(.5,.24,'$30 \\;=\\; 1 \\;\\times\\; 30$',ha='center',fontsize=13)
ax.text(.5,.10,'the core is a single cell:   $X=0$,  $U=0$,  $\\mathrm{NEC}=3$',ha='center',fontsize=9,color=RED)
ax.text(.5,.86,'macroscopic exotic matter, no preferred frame, unitary evolution',
        ha='center',fontsize=8.5,style='italic')
ax.set_xlim(0,1); ax.set_ylim(0,1)
ax.set_title('Figure 4.3   The defect collapses to one cell',loc='left',fontsize=9)
fin(fig,'f4_3.png')

# ---- 4.4 projection covariance, decomposed ----
pr=V2['projection']
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8,2.6))
ax.plot([p['coords'] for p in pr],[p['E'] for p in pr],'o-',color=INK,ms=5,lw=1.3,label='defect')
ax.plot([p['coords'] for p in pr],[p['core'] for p in pr],'s--',color=RED,ms=5,lw=1.2,label='core')
for p in pr:
    ax.annotate(f"{p['E']}",(p['coords'],p['E']),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(7,-2),fontsize=8)
    ax.annotate(f"$1\\times{p['mult']}$",(p['coords'],p['E']),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-30,2),fontsize=7,color=GREY)
ax.set_xlabel('coordinates retained'); ax.set_ylabel('cells')
ax.set_xticks([4,5,7,9]); ax.spines[['top','right']].set_visible(False); ax.legend(loc='upper left')
ax.text(.98,.06,'core invariant at 1;\nonly the multiplicity moves',transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha='right',fontsize=7.5,color=RED)
ax.set_title('Figure 4.4   The defect does not scale — the multiplicity does',loc='left',fontsize=9)
fin(fig,'f4_4.png')

# ---- NEW 2.5 the periodic table, contiguity ----
pt=V2['ptable']
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(7.2,2.2))
def grid(ax,cells,title,E,hl=None):
    for p,g in cells: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((g-.45,-p-.45),.9,.9,fc=INK,ec='none'))
    if hl:
        for p,g in hl: ax.add_patch(Rectangle((g-.45,-p-.45),.9,.9,fc=RED,ec='none',alpha=.6))
    ax.set_xlim(0,33); ax.set_ylim(-8.6,-0.4); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
    ax.set_title(title,fontsize=7.5)
    ax.text(16,-8.3,f'$E$ = {E}',ha='center',fontsize=9,color=(INK if E==0 else RED))
occ=set()
for g in (1,18): occ.add((1,g))
for p in (2,3):
    for g in [1,2,13,14,15,16,17,18]: occ.add((p,g))
for p in (4,5,6,7):
    for g in range(1,19): occ.add((p,g))
gaps=[(p,g) for p in (1,2,3) for g in range(1,19) if (p,g) not in occ]
grid(axes[0],occ,'18-column\n(period, group)',pt['E'],gaps)
from collections import defaultdict
byp=defaultdict(list)
for p,g in occ: byp[p].append(g)
contig={(p,i+1) for p,gs in byp.items() for i in range(len(gs))}
grid(axes[1],contig,'same 90 elements,\nplaced contiguously',pt['contiguous_E'])
Wj=pt['janet_widths']
janet={(r+1,i+1) for r,w in enumerate(Wj) for i in range(w)}
grid(axes[2],janet,'Janet left-step\n(row = $n+\\ell$), 120 cells',pt['janet_E'])
fig.suptitle('Figure 2.5   The 36 come from non-contiguous placement, not from the choice of period',
             y=1.05,fontsize=9)
fin(fig,'f2_5.png')

# ---- NEW 4.5 the six repairs ----
rp=V2['repairs']; base=V2['baseline_E']
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4,2.5))
labs=[r['op'] for r in rp]; vals=[(r['E'] if r['E'] is not None else 0) for r in rp]
cols=[GREY if r['E'] is None else (INK if r['E']<=base else RED) for r in rp]
y=np.arange(len(labs))
ax.barh(y,[max(v,0.6) for v in vals],color=cols,height=.55)
ax.axvline(base,color=BLUE,ls='--',lw=1)
ax.text(base*1.08,-0.75,f'baseline {base}',color=BLUE,fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_yticks(y); ax.set_yticklabels(labs,fontsize=7.5); ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xscale('symlog',linthresh=1); ax.set_xlabel('$E$ after the operation  (log)')
for i,r in enumerate(rp):
    t='n/a' if r['E'] is None else f"{r['E']}"
    ax.text(max(vals[i],0.6)*1.4,i,t,va='center',fontsize=7.5,color=cols[i])
ax.spines[['top','right']].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title('Figure 4.5   Six operations on the coordinate system. None repairs the defect.',
             loc='left',fontsize=9)
fin(fig,'f4_5.png')

# ---- NEW 4.6 objects as thresholds ----
ob=V2['objects']
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4,2.6))
y=np.arange(len(ob))
ax.barh(y,[o['cells'] for o in ob],color=[RED if o['here'] else INK for o in ob],height=.5,alpha=.85)
ax.barh(y,[o['reachable'] for o in ob],color=BLUE,height=.22)
ax.set_yticks(y); ax.set_yticklabels([f"{o['name']}\n{o['threshold']}" for o in ob],fontsize=7)
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_xlabel('cells of the index')
for i,o in enumerate(ob):

ax.spines[['top','right']].set_visible(False)
h=[plt.Line2D([0],[0],color=c,lw=5) for c in [RED,INK,BLUE]]
ax.legend(h,['available at our own profile','requires moving','reachable from here'],loc='lower right',fontsize=7)
ax.set_title('Figure 4.6   Objects are thresholds on profiles, not profiles',loc='left',fontsize=9)
fin(fig,'f4_6.png')

# ---- NEW 6.2 the ANEC coverage map ----
cv=V2['coverage']
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.8,2.5))
ax=axes[0]
ks=list(cv['per_proof'].keys()); vs=[cv['per_proof'][k] for k in ks]

' 'It is standard to say the Janet left-step table removes them by re-indexing period as n + l. ' 'That is not what does the work. Placing the same ninety elements contiguously within ' 'each period, with period untouched, gives E = 0. The defect comes from putting hydrogen at group 1 and ' 'helium at group 18 with sixteen empty cells between — an interior hole, which an upper envelope ' 'cannot cut because it must reach group 18 to admit helium.','thm')] s += [P('So the 36 do not vanish under Janet; they stop being visible. And they are not absent objects: ' '26 of them — 1p, 1d and 2d — could never hold an element, being forbidden by ' 'l ≤ n−1. They are the footprint of a law the coordinate system has no axis for. The ' 'remaining 10 are 3d, which exists and is merely deferred past 4s by the Madelung order: those are ' 'convention. The 36 is two constraints casting a thirty-six-cell shadow, not thirty-six facts.')] s += [fig('f2_5.png','Figure 2.5. Three presentations of the same chemistry. Red: cells the envelope admits and ' 'chemistry denies. Contiguity, not the choice of period, is what closes the table.')] s += [P('This makes the periodic table the control for the rest of the paper rather than an analogy. It ' 'is an arity-2 defect and therefore removable, which is what makes the violation index’s ' 'irremovability in Part IV a measurement rather than a failure to search.','note')]''' HELLY = '''s += [P('The Helly number is at least 5 and at most 144. A critical family of size five is exhibited: ' 'every four of its members intersect and the five do not. The upper bound is the ground set — all ' 'C(9,2) × 4 = 144 square directions occur, and a minimal family with empty intersection can have at ' 'most one member per omitted point. So molecular transit is not reducible to pairwise or four-wise ' 'checks, and is reducible to 144-wise, which is a bound and a useless one.','thm')] s += [P('An earlier version of this work reported the Helly number as unbounded, on the strength of a ' 'joint-given-pairwise ratio falling without saturation to m = 6. That ratio measures how often random ' 'families intersect, not the Helly number, and the inference was invalid. See Part VII.','note')]''' DEFECT = '''s += [H2('4.4 The defect, and its collapse')] s += [P(f"The index holds {V2['cells']:,} cells; its minimal network holds {V2['BPC']:,}. The defect is " f"{V2['defect']}, all of it genuine global-consistency failure — envelope coarseness " f"contributes {V2['env_coarse']}.")] s += [P('It is not thirty findings. The excess is exactly the product of a core with a multiplicity: ' 'one core cell × thirty free-coordinate configurations, and the product is exact. The thirty is not ' 'a property of the defect at all — it is the number of configurations the index itself admits ' 'alongside X = 0, U = 0, SD = 0, computed independently and matching.','thm')] s += [P('The core is one cell. (X = 0, U = 0, NEC = 3): macroscopic exotic matter, no preferred frame, ' 'unitary evolution. Coarsening the NEC axis all the way to violated or not still leaves it, and ' 'the envelope calculation says why in two lines — φ(NEC | X = 0) must permit the value ' 'because X = 0 cells with U ≥ 1 reach it, and φ(NEC | U = 0) must permit it because U = 0 ' 'cells with X ≥ 1 do. Both conditioning coordinates individually admit what the pair ' 'forbids.')] s += [fig('f4_3.png','Figure 4.3. The defect collapses to a single cell times a multiplicity.')] s += [H2('4.5 Cause, and the unique minimal support')] s += [P('The constraint the envelope cannot see is a two-payer branch. Three independent literatures give it, ' 'from unrelated starting points, and none gives a single payer: Buniy–Hsu–Murray from ' 'effective field theory; Hartman–Kundu–Tajdini from microcausality, whose theorem assumes ' 'unitary and Lorentz-invariant and interacting, so violating its conclusion breaks one of ' 'three; and Wall from the generalised second law.')] s += [P('The support is unique. Of 414 coordinate subsets that exclude {X, U, NEC}, zero fail to ' 'close. The triple is the only minimal failing subset, and every larger failure is it carried up by free ' 'coordinates. The index has arity exactly 3, with one generator.','thm')] s += [H2('4.6 The repair space is closed')] s += [P('Six distinct operations on the coordinate system were tried. None removes the defect, and each fails ' 'for a different structural reason.')] s += [tbl([['operation','outcome','why'], ['merge by identification','not licensed','no pair among {X, U, NEC} is biconditional at every rung'], ['merge by linearisation','worse','collapsing two axes forces every constraint on either through one envelope'], ['relabel axis values','never zero','exhaustive: 0 of 17,280; permutation gives an envelope no second argument'], ['slide within rows','never better','the hole is a row that should not exist, not a gap within one'], ['add a derived coordinate','worse','the operator reconstructs from cells; a defined axis inflates the box and adds nothing'], ['split an axis','neutral or worse','pins the antecedent as well as the consequent']], widths=[40*mm,24*mm,106*mm], fs=7.5)] s += [Spacer(1,4)] s += [fig('f4_5.png','Figure 4.5. Six operations, none of which repairs the defect. Dashed line: the baseline.')] s += [P('Adding fails because the box inflates; merging fails because the envelopes coarsen. Both ' 'directions are excluded, for opposite reasons, and the two-line envelope argument covers all six at ' 'once.','thm')] s += [H2('4.7 Objects are thresholds, not cells')] s += [P('The index defines by cost. An object is definable in it only if the object requires a law to break ' '— which is why a classical black hole, a vacuum solution of ordinary general relativity, is ' 'invisible to it, in the same way the energy measure is invisible.')] s += [tbl([['object','threshold','cells','here?','reachable']]+ [[o['name'],o['threshold'],f"{o['cells']:,}",('yes' if o['here'] else 'no'),f"{o['reachable']:,}"] for o in V2['objects']], widths=[52*mm,26*mm,24*mm,20*mm,26*mm], fs=7.6)] s += [Spacer(1,4)] s += [P("Of the %s cells permitting a macroscopic wormhole, %s pay with a preferred frame, %s with " "non-unitarity, %s with signalling — and %d pay with none of the three. That zero is the " "core, seen from inside." % (f"{V2['wormhole_cost']['total']:,}", f"{V2['wormhole_cost']['frame']:,}", f"{V2['wormhole_cost']['nonunitary']:,}", f"{V2['wormhole_cost']['signalling']:,}", V2['wormhole_cost']['free']),'thm')] s += [P('An evaporating black hole is available at our own profile: Hawking radiation needs pointwise NEC ' 'violation, which is the Casimir rung we occupy. It is the one object here that requires breaking a law, ' 'and we have it.')] s += [fig('f4_6.png','Figure 4.6. Objects as thresholds on profiles.')] s += [P('What this does not license. A cell is not a wormhole; permission is not existence; reachability ' 'is not achievability; and the core is not a place — none of its cells is in the index, and none ' 'overlaps the unreachable set.','note')] s += [H2('4.8 The defect does not scale')] s += [P('Projecting one index onto nested coordinate subsets gives 3, 5, 10 and 30 at four, five, seven and ' 'nine coordinates — and every one is 1 × multiplicity. The core is invariant at one ' 'cell at every resolution; only the number of free-coordinate configurations moves, which is arithmetic ' 'rather than structure. An earlier version reported the sequence itself as a scaling law; that reading ' 'is withdrawn in Part VII.')] s += [fig('f4_4.png','Figure 4.4. The core is constant; the multiplicity is what grows.')]''' out=[] i=0 while i < len(lines): L=lines[i] if L.startswith("s += [fig('f2_4.png'"): out.append(L); out.append(''); out.extend(PT_NEW.split('\n')); i+=1; continue if L.startswith("s += [P('Molecular transit has no bounded-arity surrogate."): # skip the original 2-line paragraph j=i while not lines[j].rstrip().endswith("'thm')]"): j+=1 out.extend(HELLY.split('\n')); i=j+1; continue if L.startswith("s += [H2('4.4 The defect')]"): # replace everything up to and including the f4_4 fig line j=i while not lines[j].startswith("s += [fig('f4_4.png'"): j+=1 while not lines[j].rstrip().endswith(")]"): j+=1 out.extend(DEFECT.split('\n')); i=j+1; continue out.append(L); i+=1 open('build.py','w').write('\n'.join(out)) print('sections replaced') PYEOF for s in "2.5 The periodic" "Helly number is at least 5" "4.6 The repair space" "4.7 Objects are" "4.8 The defect does not"; do printf '%-32s %s\n' "$s" "$(grep -c "$s" build.py)"; done

input.command: cd /home/claude/paper && python3 - <<'PYEOF' b=open('build.py').read(); n=0 def rep(a,c): global b,n if a in b: b=b.replace(a,c,1); n+=1; return True print('MISS:',a[:60]); return False # ---- Part VI results ---- rep("'2. A transition between universes is not expressible as one. The cost of leaving is a ternary '\n 'disjunction carrying defect 60.", "'2. A transition between universes is not expressible as one. The cost of leaving is a ternary '\n 'disjunction carrying defect 30.") b=b.replace("carrying defect 60.","carrying defect 30, which collapses to one cell.") b=b.replace("What may be carried has unbounded Helly number.","What may be carried has Helly number at least 5.") b=b.replace("3. The defect is a property, not an artefact. Projection-covariant, characterised in one '\n 'sentence, factorable as 2 × 5 × 3 × 2, located on a single named constraint, and not '\n 'repairable by a derived coordinate — an exclusion that holds for any index.", "3. The defect is one cell, and it is irremovable. Unique minimal support verified over 414 '\n 'subsets; six coordinate operations tried and all failing; 17,280 relabellings exhausted.") b=b.replace("Destination floor X = 3, U = 1, NEC = 2.","Destination floor X = 3, U = 1, NEC = 2.") # ---- Part VII : new withdrawals ---- rep(""" ['the 6/20/60 trend as reported','read across separately-built indices; required a controlled projection']],""", """ ['the 6/20/60 trend as reported','read across separately-built indices; required a controlled projection'], ['defect 60; disjunction imposed at NEC ≥ 2','the constraint is about scale: macroscopic wormholes are excluded, Planck-scale ones are not. Imposing it at the wrong rung cost 30 admissible universes and doubled the defect'], ['Helly number unbounded','a falling joint-given-pairwise ratio measures how often random families intersect, not the Helly number. True value: between 5 and 144'], ['projection-covariance as a scaling law','the defect does not scale; the core is 1 at every resolution and only the multiplicity moves'], ['X ≥ 1 → U ≥ 1 (the closed 1,404-cell variant)','the ordinary second law survives Lorentz violation — stated by the authors of the result the edge rested on'], ['instability routed to (¬U ∨ X ≥ 1)','Buniy is scoped to Lorentz-invariant theories; the second disjunct was mine, not theirs']],""") # ---- Part VIII : replace with the located finish line ---- rep("""s += [H1('Part VIII · Open')]""", """s += [H1('Part VIII · The finish line, located')] s += [P('The defect of one cell is not an open-ended uncertainty. Seven propositions were enumerated, any one of ' 'which would close the index; four were examined against the literature; and the residue is a single ' 'named conjecture.')] s += [tbl([['proposition','verdict'], ['X ≥ 1 → U ≥ 1 — Lorentz violation costs unitarity', 'refuted. Eling, Foster, Jacobson and Wall distinguish the ordinary from the generalised second law and state that the ordinary one should remain valid in Lorentz-violating theories. The chain is severed at its second link by the authors of its first.'], ['U ≥ 1 → IC = 2 — non-unitarity signals', 'refuted. The U = 1 rung is occupied: Nikolić shows high Hamiltonian degeneracy permits local, energy-momentum-conserving non-unitary evolution, and computes the Lindblad operators explicitly.'], ['NEC ≥ 3 → X ≥ 1 — exotic matter needs a preferred frame', 'refuted. Buniy’s theorem is scoped to causal, Lorentz-invariant theories; inside that scope the conclusion is instability, with no superluminal branch.'], ['NEC ≥ 3 → U ≥ 1 — exotic matter costs unitarity', 'conditional. Proven in flat space for any reasonable QFT. In curved spacetime it rests on the self-consistent achronal ANEC (Graham–Olum 2007), which is a conjecture.']], widths=[52*mm,118*mm], fs=7.5)] s += [Spacer(1,5)] s += [P('The index closes if and only if the self-consistent achronal ANEC holds in four dimensions. A ' 'holographic counterexample exists (Ishibashi, Maeda and Mefford 2019), but the same group’s later ' 'work identifies it as a conformal-frame artefact — the ANEC is not conformally invariant, so a ' 'conformal transformation can magnify a local violation — and supplies the repair, a conformally ' 'invariant ANEC. In odd boundary dimensions the repair is clean; in four dimensions the conformal anomaly ' 'leaves a weighted lower bound, which is exactly the quantity that would settle this.','thm')] s += [P('The coverage of the existing proofs can be mapped. Six proofs, indexed by geometry, field content, ' 'coupling, curvature and backreaction, cover 30 of 48 cases; the 18 uncovered are all curved with ' 'interacting or non-minimally coupled fields, and the wormhole case is among them. The count is ' 'framing-dependent — it ranges from 6 to 72 across reasonable models — but the fraction ' 'is invariant under the number of axes and moves only with how generously two specific results are read.')] s += [fig('f6_2.png','Figure 6.2. What each ANEC proof covers, and what moves the fraction left open.')] s += [P('Every curved-space proof crosses at the same place — free, minimally coupled fields — ' 'just as every path from source to target in Λ9 crosses at q, the unique articulation ' 'point separating the two halves of the lattice. Extending any single proof relaxes one pin and leaves ' 'the other, which is why eighteen years of partial results have not closed it.','note')] s += [H1('Part IX · Open')]""") open('build.py','w').write(b) print('applied',n) PYEOF for s in "Part VIII · The finish" "Part IX · Open" "Helly number unbounded" "refuted." ; do printf '%-34s %s\n' "$s" "$(grep -c "$s" build.py)"; done && timeout 900 python3 build.py 2>&1 | tail -3

**Caught up. 29 pages, 24 figures, all twenty-one audits passing.**

## What entered as findings

**The periodic table control (new §2.5).** The 36 do not vanish under Janet's re-indexing — **the same ninety elements placed contiguously, with period untouched, give E = 0.** Contiguity does the work, not n + ℓ. And the 36 decompose: 26 are the footprint of ℓ ≤ n−1 on cells no element could occupy, 10 are the Madelung convention. Two constraints casting a thirty-six-cell shadow. This makes the periodic table the **control** rather than an analogy — an arity-2 defect, therefore removable, which is what makes the violation index's irremovability a measurement.

**The collapse (§4.4).** Defect 30 = **1 × 30**, exact. One core cell, times a multiplicity that is a property of the index rather than of the defect. The core survives coarsening the NEC axis to binary.

**The unique support (§4.5).** 414 subsets excluding {X, U, NEC}; zero fail. Arity exactly 3, one generator.

**The closed repair space (§4.6).** Six operations, all failing, each for a different reason — and the two-line envelope argument covers all six.

**Objects as thresholds (§4.7).** Of 1,146 cells permitting a macroscopic wormhole, **zero** pay with none of the three payers. An evaporating black hole is available at our own profile.

**The located finish line (new Part VIII).** Three propositions refuted with sources, one conditional. The index closes iff the self-consistent achronal ANEC holds in four dimensions.

## The correction that mattered most

**I had imposed the constraint at the wrong rung.** The literature is about *scale* — macroscopic wormholes are excluded, Planck-scale ones are not. Applying the disjunction at NEC ≥ 2 cost 30 admissible universes and doubled the defect. Fixing it gives **2,370 cells, defect 30, core 1**.

Six entries added to the withdrawal register, including the 1,404-cell closed variant, the unbounded Helly claim, and projection-covariance as a scaling law.

Ready to return to the one profile.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate Transitions.md from the cached datasets, so numbers stay synced with the PDF."""
import json
D = json.load(open('/home/claude/paper/data.json'))
V2=D['v2']; T=D['tower']; O=D['order']; Q=D['quiver']; R=D['routes']
H=D['hasse']; MOL=D['molecular']; CN=D['containment']; PT=V2['ptable']; CV=V2['coverage']
f=lambda n: f'{n:,}'
FIG='figures/'

def objrow(o): return f"| {o['name']} | `{o['threshold']}` | {f(o['cells'])} | {'**yes**' if o['here'] else 'no'} | {f(o['reachable'])} |"

md = f"""# TRANSITIONS

### The closure defect of an index, and what it costs to leave a universe

**Matthew Lach** · Independent Researcher

---

**Abstract.** For a finite set of integer tuples X we compute **E(X) = |R(X)| − |X|**, where R is the closure of X
under its monotone pairwise envelopes. We prove R is a closure operator and that E ≥ 0, and we identify E = 0 with
global consistency of a binary constraint network. Applied to an atomic-structure lattice Λ of 976 cells and its
tower to {f(T['cells'][-1])}, the defect is zero at every level, verified by ambient-box sweep to
{f(T['box'][-1])} tuples; the certificates are Freuder (1982) for the tree levels and Montanari (1974) for the
monotone ones. Applied to an index of which physical laws must break to reach another universe, the defect is
**{V2['defect']}**, and it collapses exactly to **one cell times a multiplicity of thirty**. The core is a single
profile: macroscopic exotic matter with no preferred frame and unitary evolution. We show the cause is one ternary
constraint with a unique minimal support, verified over {V2['support']['subsets_checked']} coordinate subsets;
that **six distinct operations on the coordinate system all fail to repair it**, including an exhaustive search
over all {f(V2['relabel']['tested'])} axis relabellings; and that the periodic table's own defect of 36, by
contrast, vanishes under mere re-placement. A universe is a globally consistent constraint network; a transition
between universes is not expressible as one.

> **What this paper does not claim.** Nothing here bears on whether other universes exist, or whether transit
> between them is physically achievable. Every result is a statement about an *index* — what a coordinate system
> can and cannot carry. The precedent is the periodic table, whose defect of 36 is a fact about a drawing and not
> about chemistry.

![The result]({FIG}f6_1.png)

*Figure 6.1 (shown first). One object is decidable by local consistency; the two that cross between universes are
not, and for the same reason.*

---

## Contents

- [Part 0 · Procedure](#part-0--procedure)
- [Part I · The operator](#part-i--the-operator)
- [Part II · Λ verified](#part-ii--λ-verified)
- [Part III · Transit structures on Λ](#part-iii--transit-structures-on-λ)
- [Part IV · The violation index](#part-iv--the-violation-index)
- [Part V · The multilattice](#part-v--the-multilattice)
- [Part VI · Results](#part-vi--results)
- [Part VII · Register of withdrawals](#part-vii--register-of-withdrawals)
- [Part VIII · The finish line, located](#part-viii--the-finish-line-located)
- [Part IX · Open](#part-ix--open)
- [Appendix A · Equations](#appendix-a--equations)
- [Appendix B · References and sources](#appendix-b--references-and-sources)
- [Appendix C · Verification](#appendix-c--verification)

---

## Part 0 · Procedure

The protocols below were in force throughout and are reported because several results in this paper are
corrections of earlier results obtained without them.

### 0.1 Protocols

| protocol | |
|---|---|
| commit before looking | a position is written down before any retrieval; the retrieval scores it |
| compute before writing | numerical claims are computed, then reported, never the reverse |
| refuse rather than coerce | an ambiguous instruction is queried, not defaulted |
| enumerate before searching | targets are listed before the first search and re-listed when the set grows |
| record what a failure excludes | a falsified prediction is logged with the class of claim it rules out |

### 0.2 The Admission Law

> An open index admits any content, and admits it only together with its verification grade. An entry's grade
> bounds the operations it may enter. **A derived entry carries the minimum grade of its inputs, and no derivation
> raises a grade.** Content contradicting the index is admitted and flagged as a collision; a collision is
> discharged by re-deriving the internal result, never by refusing the content.

The last clause matters. An index that refuses contradicting content closes itself against exactly the information
that would correct it. Every substantive repair in this work arrived as a collision. The bibliography in Appendix B
carries an access grade per source for the same reason.

### 0.3 The merge rule

Five coordinate merges were attempted. One was licensed by a stated biconditional; four by a one-way implication or
an intuitive ordering. All four failed, and the survivor failed under grading.

| merge | basis | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| cloning ≡ discrimination | stated biconditional | holds at the perfect rung only |
| nonlinearity → signalling | one-way implication | failed — Polchinski nonlinearities do not signal |
| microcausality → signalling | one-way implication | failed — converse denied by Sorkin scenarios |
| signalling on the CHSH scale | intuitive ordering | failed — PR boxes reach 4 without signalling |
| discrimination into correlation | intuitive ordering | failed — different quantities |

> **Rule.** A biconditional licenses a merge only if it holds at every rung of the graded axis. Merging on a fact
> true at one point and then grading the axis is the error.

### 0.4 Operator reliability, measured

Prediction accuracy was tracked by target class rather than assumed uniform. Predictions aimed at logical structure
— which hypotheses a theorem takes, which way an entailment runs, what a conclusion licenses — scored 4/4 on three
consecutive tests. Predictions aimed at how a field regards a claim scored 1/4. Predictions of implications not yet
in the index scored about 1 in 5. Under 0.2 the last class was therefore barred from entering content: every clause
in Part IV was entered from retrieval, never from assessment.

---

## Part I · The operator

### 1.1 Definitions

For a finite X ⊆ ∏Aᵢ of integer tuples, write **Âᵢ(X) = {{xᵢ : x ∈ X}}** for the value sets and
**φ̂ᵢⱼ(v) = max{{xᵢ : x ∈ X, xⱼ ≤ v}}** for the monotone upper envelope of coordinate i against coordinate j.
Then R(X) collects every point of the observed product box respecting all envelopes, and E(X) is its excess.
Equations (1)–(4) of Appendix A give these in full. No outside knowledge enters R(X): it is what a reader could
reconstruct from the cells alone.

### 1.2 Proposition. X ⊆ R(X), hence E ≥ 0

> *Proof.* Let x ∈ X. Each xᵢ ∈ Âᵢ(X) by definition. For any i ≠ j the set {{yᵢ : y ∈ X, yⱼ ≤ xⱼ}} contains xᵢ,
> since x satisfies xⱼ ≤ xⱼ. Hence φ̂ᵢⱼ(xⱼ) ≥ xᵢ, so x ∈ R(X). ∎

The word *defect* is therefore justified: E counts cells the structure admits and the index denies, and can never
count in the other direction.

### 1.3 Proposition. R is a closure operator

Extensive by 1.2. Monotone and idempotent by computation: R(R(X)) = R(X) on Λ₈ and on the violation index;
monotonicity held on thirty nested random pairs with no failure. The closed sets therefore form a Moore family.

### 1.4 Identification

R is the closure of a binary constraint network under monotone binary projections, and **E(X) = 0 if and only if
the network is globally consistent** — every tuple satisfying all binary projections is a solution.

### 1.5 R against the full minimal network

Writing BPC(X) for closure under the *full* binary projections rather than their monotone envelopes,
X ⊆ BPC(X) ⊆ R(X) — equation (5). So E > 0 is in principle ambiguous between genuine inconsistency and envelope
coarseness. Computed for both objects here, **the ambiguity does not arise**: R = BPC exactly, so R is the minimal
network and the whole defect is global-consistency failure.

![Nested sets]({FIG}f1_1.png)

*Figure 1.1. For Λ₈ all three coincide at 976. For the violation index X = {f(V2['cells'])} while
BPC = R = {f(V2['R'])} — {V2['defect']} tuples in the minimal network that are not solutions, and
{V2['env_coarse']} envelope coarseness.*

### 1.6 Six blindnesses

| blind to | instance | effect on E |
|---|---|---|
| decreasing bounds (exclusion) | a preferred frame forbids chronology violation | 0 → 6 |
| non-monotone relations (congruence) | seniority parity on axis 10 | 0 → 678 |
| multi-coordinate (ternary) constraints | conjugation ceiling / coupling triangle | 186 / 35,570 |
| unoccupied dimensions | a fifth axis nothing occupies | unchanged |
| the measure | two universes, same cells, different energies | unchanged |
| derived coordinates | an axis defined as a function of others | {V2['defect']} → 120 |

**A derived coordinate cannot repair closure.** R reconstructs from cells alone, so a reader given the cells cannot
see that a coordinate was *defined* as a function of others; meanwhile the ambient box grows by that coordinate's
value count while |X| stays fixed. This excludes the entire class of derived-coordinate repairs, for any index.

![Blindness panels]({FIG}f1_2.png)

*Figure 1.2. What an upper envelope cannot cut. Black: solutions. Red: admitted by R, denied by the constraint.*

### 1.7 The closure rule

> **A tightening preserves E = 0 if and only if it binds one coordinate by a monotone function of one other.**

![Closure rule]({FIG}f1_3.png)

*Figure 1.3. Four tightenings of the lattice, two on each side of the rule.*

### 1.8 Named theorems

| result | statement |
|---|---|
| Freuder 1982 | a tree-structured constraint network is globally consistent after arc consistency |
| Montanari 1974 | for monotone constraints, path consistency implies global consistency |
| van Beek & Dechter 1995 | generalisation of monotone to row-convex constraints |
| van Beek & Dechter 1997 | constraint tightness — the exact/admissible ratio |

These two theorems cover the lattice between them: Λ₉ is a tree and every level is monotone. Neither applies to the
violation index, which is neither.

---

## Part II · Λ verified

Λ is an atomic-structure lattice. Cells are 8-tuples (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S) built by nested bounds — equations
(6)–(12). The tower Λ₉–Λ₁₃ adds target spin, seniority, the core's J, K and the outer J, equations (13)–(17).
Caps (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1) are unique in the search range for 976 cells.

### 2.1 The tower closes at every level

| level | {' | '.join(str(l) for l in T['level'])} |
|---|{'---|'*len(T['level'])}
| cells | {' | '.join(f(c) for c in T['cells'])} |
| ambient box | {' | '.join(f(b) for b in T['box'])} |
| E | {' | '.join('0' for _ in T['level'])} |

Every level was swept against its entire ambient box, to {f(T['box'][-1])} tuples at Λ₁₃. Global consistency in the
strict sense also holds: |BPC(Λ₈)| = 976 = |Λ₈|.

![The tower]({FIG}f2_1.png)

*Figure 2.1. Cells and ambient box diverge on a log scale while E stays zero.*

### 2.2 Why it closes

Λ₉'s constraint graph has nine nodes and eight edges and is a tree, so Freuder applies. Λ₉′ — the same lattice with
the admissible Pauli cut 2S′ ≤ 2f+1, which removes 93 cells, leaving {f(T['L9prime'])} — gains the cycle f–g–2S′
and loses the guarantee. Λ₁₀ has ten nodes and ten edges and is also not a tree, so **Λ₉ is the last tree level**.

![Constraint graphs]({FIG}f2_2.png)

*Figure 2.2. One added edge converts a tree into a cycle.*

### 2.3 Where the exactness goes

All six density values reproduce once three non-obvious exact sets are used: the spin set of f^g by microstate
enumeration at axis 9; terms genuinely *new* at occupancy v, conjoined with the parity congruence and the
conjugation ceiling, at axis 10; and the J values of terms of ℓᵏ carrying the cell's own multiplicity 2S at axis 11.

## Part VIII · The finish line, located

The defect of one cell is not an open-ended uncertainty. Seven propositions were enumerated, any one of which would
close the index; four were examined against the literature; and the residue is a single named conjecture.

| proposition | verdict |
|---|---|
| X ≥ 1 → U ≥ 1 — Lorentz violation costs unitarity | **refuted.** Eling, Foster, Jacobson and Wall distinguish the ordinary from the generalised second law and state that the ordinary one should remain valid in Lorentz-violating theories. The chain is severed at its second link by the authors of its first. |
| U ≥ 1 → IC = 2 — non-unitarity signals | **refuted.** The U = 1 rung is occupied: Nikolić shows high Hamiltonian degeneracy permits local, energy-momentum-conserving non-unitary evolution, and computes the Lindblad operators explicitly. |
| NEC ≥ 3 → X ≥ 1 — exotic matter needs a preferred frame | **refuted.** Buniy's theorem is scoped to causal, Lorentz-invariant theories; inside that scope the conclusion is instability, with no superluminal branch. |
| NEC ≥ 3 → U ≥ 1 — exotic matter costs unitarity | **conditional.** Proven in flat space for any reasonable QFT. In curved spacetime it rests on the self-consistent achronal ANEC (Graham–Olum 2007), which is a conjecture. |

> **The index closes if and only if the self-consistent achronal ANEC holds in four dimensions.** A holographic
> counterexample exists (Ishibashi, Maeda and Mefford 2019), but the same group's later work identifies it as a
> conformal-frame artefact — the ANEC is not conformally invariant, so a conformal transformation can magnify a
> local violation — and supplies the repair, a conformally invariant ANEC. In odd boundary dimensions the repair is
> clean; in four dimensions the conformal anomaly leaves a weighted lower bound, which is exactly the quantity that
> would settle this.

Six proofs, indexed by geometry, field content, coupling, curvature and backreaction, cover **{CV['covered']} of
{CV['cases']}** cases; the {CV['uncovered']} uncovered are all curved with interacting or non-minimally coupled
fields, and the wormhole case is among them. The count is framing-dependent — it ranges from 6 to 72 across
reasonable models — but the *fraction* is invariant under the number of axes and moves only with how generously two
